notes.meaning: God told Moses to lead a holy war against the Midianites before his life ended. Midian had tricked Israel into worshiping false idols and committing sexual sins at Baal Peor. Being 'gathered to your people' meant Moses was about to die, resting from his earthly work and joining the faithful who went before him.

Moses promptly carried out God's command and told the people to prepare for battle. While God spoke of avenging Israel, Moses called it avenging the Lord, showing that God's honor and the people's safety were tied together. Israel was not acting out of personal hatred, but as ministers carrying out God's righteous sentence.

Moses ordered each of the twelve tribes to send one thousand soldiers, creating an army of twelve thousand men. Calling an equal number from every tribe kept the tribes united and prevented jealousy. This small force against a large enemy taught Israel to trust in God's power rather than their own numbers.

Moses sent Phinehas, the priest's son, with the army instead of sending him as a military general. Phinehas had already shown great boldness against Midian's sins at Peor, making him well suited to provide spiritual guidance. He brought sacred instruments and silver trumpets to signal that God was with them in battle.

The Israelite army attacked Midian just as the Lord had commanded and struck down every adult male combatant they encountered. This destruction applied to the local Midianite clans that had plotted against Israel, rather than the entire race scattered in distant lands. God gave them a decisive victory without losing a single soldier.

The Israelites killed the five rulers of the Midianite regions, including Zur, the father of Cozbi who had lured Israel into sin. They also put the prophet Balaam to death with the sword. Balaam had sought greedy gain by showing Midian how to corrupt Israel, and God's providence brought him to the place of his judgment.

The troops captured the Midianite women and children and gathered all their livestock and goods as plunder. They also burned down all their settlements and camps. Setting fire to these sites wiped out places of idolatry and stopped any survivors from rebuilding a hostile power there.

The soldiers brought all the captives, animals, and goods directly back to Moses, Eleazar the priest, and the congregation. The camp was situated on the plains of Moab across the Jordan River from Jericho. Instead of keeping the spoil for themselves right away, the army showed humble obedience by letting God's leaders oversee its division.

Moses, Eleazar, and the tribal leaders went out of the camp to meet the returning troops. This honored the soldiers publicly for risking their lives in battle for the nation. Meeting them outside also kept the camp pure, since anyone who had touched death was ritually unclean.

Moses was angry with the army officers for sparing the grown women. He reminded them that these were the very individuals who followed Balaam's advice and seduced the Israelites into worshiping Baal of Peor, which brought a deadly plague upon Israel. Sparing the source of that moral downfall put the nation's spiritual life in grave danger once again.

Moses commanded the troops to put to death every woman who had been with a man, along with every young boy. The adult women were executed for actively enticing Israel into rebellion against God, and the boys were put to death to prevent the idolatrous nation from rising again in revenge. Only the young girls were spared, as they had taken no part in the sin at Peor and could be brought safely into God's covenant community.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some historical critics view this story as a later legend created to reflect early war ideals, while others see it as a factual ancient account of severe tribal warfare commanded under the theocratic order.

notes.meaning: Anyone who had killed a person or touched a dead body was ordered to stay outside the camp for seven days. They were required to wash and purify themselves, their prisoners, and their goods on the third and seventh days. Even though the war was commanded by God, contact with death made someone ceremonially unclean, showing that human life is sacred.

Eleazar the priest gave the religious rules for cleansing the physical goods captured from the Midianites. Hard metals like gold, silver, bronze, iron, tin, and lead had to pass through fire and then be washed with special purification water. Anything that could not endure fire had to be washed in water so that items used in pagan worship could be dedicated to God.

The soldiers had to wash their clothes on the seventh day to complete their cleansing. Once this week of separation and washing was done, they were welcomed back into the main camp. This showed that God's people must put aside all defilement before entering His presence.

The Lord told Moses, Eleazar, and the tribal heads to make an exact count of all the captured animals and people. God commanded that the plunder be split evenly between the twelve thousand soldiers who fought and the rest of the congregation who stayed behind. This arrangement rewarded the fighters for their hardships while reminding everyone that the victory belonged to the whole nation.
